speakeroldname: Mr. Ambrose Hubert Peddle (Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador):
subtopic: MR. PEDDLE-FORGERY OF SIGNATURE ON PASSES TO MEMBERS' GALLERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege concerning the matter to which Your Honour has already referred. It is a personal question of privilege-or is it a question of personal privilege-arising out of the abuse of the privileges of this House which occurred in the galleries of the House yesterday and which was only controlled when Your Honour adjourned the House.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
I am informed that certain of these persons who created the disturbance were admitted to the members' galleries by the security guards on presenting admission cards purporting to bear my signature. If I had, in fact, signed these cards I would be in part responsible to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the House for the conduct of these persons in abusing the privileges of the House. I assure you, Sir, and I assure the members of the House that I did not sign these cards. My name was signed to these cards without my authority, and my signature was in each instance forged.
Forgery is a crime, and this House has never intruded its authority into the administration of the criminal law. It has properly left the investigation of crime and the prosecution of crime to the police-municipal, provincial and federal as the case may be. Forgery is a crime under the Criminal Code and is within the jurisdiction of the RCMP. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I advise you of my intention to report the forgery of my name in these instances to the RCMP, and to request the RCMP to investigate the circumstances under which, and by whom, my name was forged.
Undoubtedly, Sir, the RCMP officers will have to ask the assistance of yourself, Mr. Speaker, in the interrogation of officers and employees of this House who are under your
May 12, 1970

Procedure and Organization direction, and for this reason I consider it my duty and a matter of courtesy to you to inform you of my intention.

speechtext:

subsubtopic: REDUCTION OF BANK OF CANADA REDISCOUNT RATE-EFFECT ON CREDIT SUPPLY AND CANADIAN DOLLAR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I have indicated previously the rate of the Bank of Canada, the rediscount rate, this particular lending rate is not used very often, and it seemed appropriate under the circumstances to reduce it by half of one per cent, which the Governor of the Bank of Canada decided to do after, of course, consultation with me.

speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. The minister has not given any indication as to the purpose of this, but will he agree that the effect of the total package, the increase in the reserve requirements for the commercial banks and the additional treasury bills being sold to the banks, will have the effect of substantially tightening the supply of credit in the country?

subsubtopic: REDUCTION OF BANK OF CANADA REDISCOUNT RATE-EFFECT ON CREDIT SUPPLY AND CANADIAN DOLLAR
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, they should be completely offsetting.

subsubtopic: REDUCTION OF BANK OF CANADA REDISCOUNT RATE-EFFECT ON CREDIT SUPPLY AND CANADIAN DOLLAR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is not the sort of thing one can pursue too far by way of question and answer. It is more appropriate perhaps to ask the minister if he would consider reverting to motions in order to make a statement to explain this very puzzling action to the country. The minister says on the one hand that the reduction in the bank rate is expected to have virtually no effect and then he says it is going to offset some other effects. Would the minister consider making a statement on motions?

subsubtopic: REDUCTION OF BANK OF CANADA REDISCOUNT RATE-EFFECT ON CREDIT SUPPLY AND CANADIAN DOLLAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think it is necessary to revert to motions. It is a very simple matter. The offsetting effect was not the reduction in the interest rate but rather the increase in the secondary reserves of the banks which will offset the additional amount that would go into the money supply due to the issuing of the additional treasury bills which have become necessary because of the strength of the Canadian dollar.

Mr. Speaker, on the third reading of this bill to set up a law reform commission, I might say to the House that, with the exception of a few amendments, the members of the committee were in accord that this is a good commission to set up. However, I wish to deal with one or two points. I hope that this commission would not be established and used by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) or the government for the purpose of procrastinating in respect of reforms that are obvious. I should like to draw an analogy.
What happened yesterday in the gallery with reference to the law of abortion arose because an incorrect impression was left when the omnibus bill came up in the House. If you were to go back to the record of my speeches you would find that I had pointed out then that the abortion law of Canada was not being changed. Under the original code a therapeutic abortion was permitted under certain circumstances where there was a danger to the life of a mother, and this was left to the discretion of the professional medical practitioner. The courts interpreted that as meaning not only when the life of the mother was endangered but also when her health was in danger. So, in that regard, the law has not been changed at all. Those people who pressed for abortion reform were led to believe by various people, and even by the ministers who took part in the debate, that
DEBATES	6855
Law Reform Commission Bill there would be a great reform in the abortion law. Females across this country who wished to exercise what they thought was their new legal right found to their surprise that the law had not been reformed. In fact, in my opinion, the amended law curtails the right to therapeutic abortion. I believe that is the reason for the degree of excitement and emotional disturbance which took place yesterday in the galleries of the House of Commons.
The analogy I want to draw is this. We passed a bill called the omnibus Criminal Code reform bill, about which much was written by the press of the country and much was said through the various communications media. The bill was described as a great reform measure and a step forward in many directions. I said then, and I repeat now, that so far as most matters covered by that bill were concerned there was no reform whatsoever. People were fooled and deceived. I imagine that the people who wrote articles about the bill and the newspapers which printed them, really believed there was going to be reform.
Unless one were a lawyer and analysed the amendments as they were written in the Criminal Code reform bill, one would not have appreciated, at the time of the debate, the fact that there was actually no reform so far as abortion was concerned. What I am saying is I do hope that when this new commission is set up it will not be used to procrastinate so far as reform is concerned or that an alternative will not be used to bluff the public that they are getting the reform when in fact this is not the case at all.
To what sections of the Criminal Code can reforms be proposed? Under the Criminal Code of Canada any person seven years or older, provided he understands the nature and quality of the act, can be charged and convicted, and any child over the age of 14, without the previously stated qualification, can be charged. There was a private member's bill before the House under my name which dealt with that subject but which was deliberately talked out. The Solicitor General (Mr. Mcllraith) has just taken his place, so let me point this out to him. The rumour I heard-and he can deny it-is that he told his backbenchers not to let the reform go through, not because it was a bad reform but because it came from the wrong side of the House.

I do hope that this commission will not use this method to procrastinate in bringing about the necessary reform. What are some of the other reforms? I just returned from a conference on law reform which several professors from various law schools across the country attended. The conference was held at Cedar Glen on Thursday and Friday of last week. Some top men in the field were present, such as Hogarth of Osgood Hall. I am sure that the former dean of Saskatchewan university wiU give a sympathetic hearing to some of the suggestions I will make. He pointed out that although there is not one law for the rich and one for the poor, that is the case in its application.
Let us consider bail, for example. Members from all sides of the House have been asking for some reform in the law as it applies to bail. Only two weeks ago, in Banff, Alberta, three young men were picked up on a drug charge. Two of them, who were from affluent families, were granted bail on Sunday morning. The third, who was from a poor family, remained in jail. So, there is discrimination. The three young men were charged with the same offence. What do our young men think of a society in which two people who come from affluent families can be left free while their trial is pending, a trial which may not take place until next fall after the case goes through a preliminary hearing, while the third remains in jail? Fortunately, the two young men went out amongst high school and university students and personally raised enough money to bail out the young man who did not have a rich family behind him. In many cases this does not happen. The point I am making is that I hope this law commission will not just be a piece of window dressing. I hope that when we ask the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner), the Solicitor General or anyone else connected with the administration of law a question in the House with regard to reform of the law, they will not say that it is before the law reform commission. I hope this Commission will not be just another excuse for an all-powerful government, with an all-powerful bureaucracy behind it, to hide and procrastinate on the reforms that are needed.
The next matter with which I wish to deal concerns the question of drugs. I heard a newscast the other day which I found very interesting. Members from all sides of the House have been asking for the LeDain Commission report on the drug problem which is one of the most serious social questions

Canada is facing today in relation to the young people in high schools, universities and elsewhere. I listened to the newscast in which it was suggested that there has been some interference by members of this government, by cabinet ministers, with the work of the LeDain Commission. Mr. Speaker, we in the New Democratic Party are very happy that Bill C-186 has reached third reading stage. We supported it on second reading and also in committee.
In Canada we are not law pacers; we are law followers. When we talk about the law reform commission we should remember that the State of New York set up its law reform commission in 1934. New Zealand established its law reform commission in 1937; California established its in 1953; Ontario established its commission in 1964, and England established its law reform commission in 1965. That is a clear indication that we are following the pattern set by other countries rather than setting the pace.
The Ontario Law Reform Commission had great success in studying certain aspects of the law. It has done a great job with regard to the Mechanics Lien Act, personal property security and expropriation, and it would be fair to say that with regard to expropriation it set the pattern for the federal act.
We look with encouragement at the law reform commission that is being established. At committee stage the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) said that certain matters would be referred to it. He said that probably the first matters would be the Criminal Code and the Evidence Act. These two matters do go together but, Mr. Speaker, I would hope that even though the commission may be studying them in depth it will not overlook the report
May 12, 1970

Law Reform Commission Bill of the Canadian Committee on Corrections, commonly called the Ouimet Commission Report. If we were to use the balance of this session to implement the recommendations contained in the Ouimet Commission Report we would be faced with a heavy workload in our endeavours to up-date the criminal law and reform institutions in Canada.
In committee, the minister also said that he hopes before this session ends to introduce a bill dealing with bail procedures, and procedures on arrest. He also indicated that he might introduce amendments with regard to vagrancy. I hope that he will implement one of the recommendations of the Ouimet Commission concerning corporal punishment. These are all matters that should be dealt with by the end of this session, and by the beginning of next session the minister and the Solicitor General (Mr. Mcllraith) could combine to introduce legislation implementing the balance of the Ouimet Commission recommendations. It is one thing to refer the Criminal Code and the Evidence Act to a committee, and ask it to study the different areas of the Criminal Code in depth, but it is another matter to have the committee study the philosophy relating to criminal law. I hope that the Law Reform Commission will study the philosophy relating to criminal law.
The time has come when we must closely examine the adversary system as it relates to criminal law. We have made an improvement in the treatment of juvenile delinquents. Here, the basis of approach is one of rehabilitation or reformation, and it has worked quite successfully. I hope we can carry over this approach into criminal law, and lessen the emphasis on the adversary system.
I am sure that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Cantin) would enjoy hearing parts of a speech which the Minister of Justice delivered in Windsor, when the minister attacked the adversary system, particularly certain myths that prevail with regard to it. With respect to three of those myths he said:
We must disabuse ourselves of the myth that the criminal law process can be understood within the contours of the adversary system.
We must disabuse ourselves of the myth that there is indeed an adversary system of criminal justice at all.
We must disabuse ourselves of the myth that the criminal law sanction falls with equal impact on all segments of society.
He set forth the differences between vagrancy and public drunkenness to demonstrate the third myth.

I recall that when I introduced a bill designed to abolish corporal punishment, the Parliamentary Secretary spoke in support of it. I am sure that with this forward-looking parliamentary secretary, and with our forward-looking Minister of Justice, not only will the recommendations in the Ouimet Commission Report be implemented but they will also see to it that the law reform commission studies the Criminal Code and the Evidence Act as well as the philosophy behind them. When the commission reports, they will see that its recommendations are implemented with speed.

Mr. Speaker, when he reads today's Hansard the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner), who is away on other official business, will surely appreciate the hon. members' contribution to this debate.
It takes some time to incorporate into legislation any philosophy and commonly held ideas. This act tends, among other things, to set up the machinery which will make it possible to incorporate more quickly into law what we preach, although not overnight. This bill provides for the creation of a federal commission for the reform of laws. It is the present Minister of Justice who was the first to talk about it in October 1968, while speaking to members of the Law Society of Upper Canada convened in a special meeting at Osgoode Hall. In fact he said:
I hope that we shall soon be able to create a national commission for the reform of laws in order to explore continuously rather than occasionally the possibilities ... of amending laws.
Stating that the advance of technology and urban development was essentially reflected in the transformation of economic, social and family obligations, Mr. Turner pointed out that it would be high time to undertake, in the legal field, an orderly review and updating of the statutes. The more and more frequent intervention of the government into daily life is evidenced in the increasing number of laws passed from one year to another. Besides, the phenomenon had been already foreseen twenty years ago by the late Professor R. McGregor Dawson. This is what he said, and I quote:
Each year, the government asserts even more its authority, expands more and more the field of its activity.
May 12, 1970

To that, the present Minister of Justice answered:
It often happens that owing to special and continuous pressure to which the administrative process is submitted, many statutes or other legal regulations which control the relationship between the subjects themselves or between the subjects and the government escape this orderly review without which they will not remain consistent with either equity or changing customs.
To meet the complexity of the relationships that characterize modern societies, permanent boards of law reform have been established in certain jurisdictions. That is the context in which this legislation must be considered.
The objects of the Commission are to study and keep under review on a continuing and systematic basis the statutes and other laws of Canada with a view to making recommendations for their improvement. I am thinking here of the views expressed by the previous speaker about the updating and the review of such laws.
Without restricting the general scope of the aforementioned objects, the Commission's prime duty will be to remove anachronisms and anomalies in the laws; to reflect in and by the laws the distinctive concepts and institutions of common law, civil law, and to reconcile, in the expression and application of the law, the differences and discrepancies arising out of the differences in those concepts and institutions.
It will also have to ensure the repeal of obsolete legislation and the development of new legal concepts in keeping with the changing needs of modern Canadian society and of individual members of that society.
One hopes that the Commission will make it possible to achieve the following goals:
Firstly, to give the government an objective machinery to review federal laws;
Secondly, to create an institution to which the public may direct the serious grievances it sometimes has with respect to some federal laws;
Thirdly, to give the cabinet the means to assess proposals which are submitted to it in order to amend existing laws or to pass new ones.
Fourthly, to set up a body that will carry out a critical study of the federal laws, in the light of both common Law and civil law.
This bill provides for the establishment of a Commission of six members. The chairman, vice-chairman and two other full-time members will be appointed for a term not exceeding seven years and the two part-time mem-
Law Reform Commission Bill bers for a term not exceeding three years. It should be noted that the legislation will not require that the members of this Commission be lawyers or judges. Its provisions are broad enough to allow for the appointment of members from other professions.
The Commission, with its modest staff, will be empowered not only to carry out an exhaustive survey of the present federal laws but also to engage on a temporary basis for specific projects the services of persons having specialized knowledge in some legal field. Although the Commission will deal only with matters that come under the jurisdiction of Parliament, it will nevertheless be possible for it to co-operate with provincial, and even foreign, boards with which it could pool its knowledge or its resources, for the benefit of law reform.
The Commission will be free to conduct its own research programs. However, so as to ascertain that it will look only into matters of public interest, it will have to submit reports to Parliament and to the public through the Minister of Justice.
Finally, I may say that this legislation was unanimously approved by the members of the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs who made an in-depth study of this bill.
No doubt that this legislation is evidence that the government is anxious to undertake a reform, that will be both serious and continuous, of the federal laws.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR RELIEF OF CONVICTED PERSONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is probably a good idea, before we conclude debate on this bill, that we review exactly what has been done and, in particular, the status of the law with respect to pardons in Canada today.
The subject of pardons has, for centuries, been part of the English law and has subsequently been carried from the English to the Canadian law. A pardon has always been granted under the exercise of the royal prerogative of mercy. For years, regardless of the power of Parliament, the monarchy has reserved unto itself the power of forgiving the subject and waiving the consequences of any particular offence, as well as the power to declare that that offence has in fact never taken place. In ancient times and during the development of the monarchy, this right was exercised solely by the monarch on four bases. It was exercised under the great seal of the realm, and in that form it now is rarely exercised. It was exercised when it was found that the subject of the prosecution was innocent; when it was found that, as a result of fresh evidence, there was serious doubt as to whether the offender had committed the act in question. In earlier times, when prisons were nothing more than dungeons, it was exercised when the imprisonment of the offender would mean the loss of his life and when the offender had gone to the assistance of the penal authorities in order to repel attacks against them.
The bill that we have before us represents a great advance over the ancient prerogative of the monarchy. From time to time statute law has removed these ancient powers of the monarch and delegated them, in Canada, in a very small measure to the courts, but in the main to the Governor General in Council. Now, the provisions governing the law of pardon are contained in sections 655 and 658 of our Criminal Code.
Apart from the provisions we have before us, there exist today four types of pardon in Canada. First, there is the reservation of Her Majesty s' right to grant the royal prerogative of mercy on any occasion, which sometimes manifests itself as an amnesty granted during a royal visit or on other state occasions.
Criminal Records
Second, there is a free pardon which is granted by the Governor in Council to those who have been subsequently shown to be innocent of the offence or offences for which they were convicted, and that completely nullifies the conviction and all its consequences. Third, there is the type of pardon known as "the commutation of the death sentence", which provides that the Governor in Council may commute the death sentence to imprisonment for a term of years or to life imprisonment. Fourth, there is a conditional pardon which does not remove the stigma of the conviction but which relieves the offender of the consequences thereof.
Under the present policy of our government, most pardons granted are conditional. In practice, the Solicitor General grants pardons on the recommendation of the National Parole Board, and nothing that we have before us in the bill we are considering today will change or qualify rights which are enshrined in the Criminal Code. These forms of pardon will continue to exist regardless of the provisions of the Criminal Records Act with which we are concerned.
[DOT] (3:40 pm.)
The impetus that is behind the present change arises from the fact that even though a man may pay his debt to society, the cross of that conviction follows him all the days of his life. Depending largely on the seriousness of the offence or the number of offences of which he has been convicted, his record can crop up from time to time and plague him in many different ways, regardless of the exemplary life he may live. Unfortunately with modern methods of recording criminal convictions such as fingerprinting, photography, teletype and the many means of communication between the public and the police as well as among the police forces, and with some other nefarious methods of investigation which I hope are never conducted by government authorities, the record of a conviction lives long after the appropriate punishment has been administered. It comes up in credit applications, employment applications and visa applications. It comes up should a subsequent arrest take place. It comes up in casual conversation and certainly, at times, has even crept into extortion bids. When it does arise it can totally destroy the morale of any person who has the intention of living as a good person, regardless of what he has done in the past. The situation has been the concern of many members of this House.

May 12, 1970
Criminal Records
The occasion should not pass without mentioning the name of the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. The hon. member for Welland (Mr. Tolmie) in the past has not only presented private members' bills with respect to this subject, but has openly advocated and lobbied for reform. The problems obviously facing the government when deciding the policies contained in the bill were, in substance, twofold. First, should a pardon be automatic upon the expiration of a given number of years after the penalty has been paid? Second, in what manner and to what extent can the problem be solved from a practical point of view and with due regard to the administration of justice? To say, on the one hand, that all criminal records that are concerned with an offence which is the subject of a pardon should be erased after a given number of years is one thing, but to be able to do it by practical legislation is another. The bill before us does not provide for an automatic pardon.
The committee heard evidence from the Chairman of the National Parole Board and senior officers of the RCMP. It was quite obvious that an automatic pardon was hardly in the interest of justice. The committee, therefore, accepted the principle of pardons of the nature set out in this bill, namely, that pardon should be granted only after the expiration of a given number of years. This period was set at five years for indictable offences and two years for summary conviction offences. In addition, pardons were to be granted only after an investigation by the National Parole Board into the character of the applicant and the reputation he has enjoyed and developed in the community since the date of the completion of his sentence. This will ensure that those persons who continually choose the company of criminals, whether convicted of an offence or not, do not receive the benefit of the royal prerogative of mercy under this bill. It is specifically designed for those who can truly be said to have rehabilitated themselves from the offence or offences committed in the past. On this principle, I think it is safe to say that there was general agreement in the committee.
A pardon that is granted pursuant to this bill will indicate on the face of that document that an investigation has been made, that the applicant has been found to have been of good behaviour and is thereby pardoned from the offence or offences therein set forth. The effect of the pardon is to vacate the convic-

tion, leaving the applicant as much as possible free of the scar of the past. There was a great deal of discussion in committee which hinged on how far we could go from a practical point of view. The hon. member for Windsor-Walker ville (Mr. MacGuigan) proposed amendments, supported by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert), which, in effect, would have destroyed a record of criminal convictions for which pardons had been granted.
Although these amendments were certainly well motivated, it was obvious that legislation could not possibly be effective when consideration was given to the vast number of places in which the Parliament of Canada generally has control and where the record might be preserved. The result was that the bill was left in the same language in which it was presented to the House. The destruction of criminal records and the sealing of judicial records remained entirely within the jurisdiction of the Solicitor General (Mr. Mcllraith), those that are so closely controlled and those in the hands of the federal authorities only.
Incidental amendments of note were made in committee. For those following the bill who do not have the committee proceedings, the offences were divided into indictable and summary conviction. Pardons were to be granted after five years for indictable convictions and after two years for summary convictions. The applicant has the right to appear before the National Parole Board to make representations as to why he should get a pardon. In this instance, it will be interesting to see the effect that application has in relation to sections 18 and 28 of the new Federal Courts Act. In addition to those amendments, we provided for any disqualifications to which the applicant was subjected by statute by virtue of his conviction now having been removed.
One of the most important modifications made in committee was that no application form for employment for any position over which the federal government has jurisdiction can contain a question as to whether an applicant has been convicted of an offence if a pardon has been granted for such an offence. It is interesting to note that this applies to the written application form only. It does not preclude the employer, in conversation with his prospective employee, from asking questions of this nature. It was probably in this latter field where the work of the committee has strayed the furthest from what might be said to be the ideal. The greatest
May 12, 1970

difficulty that offenders have in our society today is procuring employment. Employers, to a large extent, still refuse to run the risk of employing someone who has offended the criminal law. The committee found, and I think it is generally agreed, that it is impossible to legislate that employers shall take this risk.
One of the most difficult decisions facing an offender, no matter how straight he has gone after his conviction, is whether upon application for a job he should tell his prospective employer about his past. If he does, very often he will not get the job. If he does not, very often he will lose his job when the employer finds out. The provisions of the present bill do not do as much as we might wish in assisting the applicant in his dilemma, but they do add a basis upon which something can be established. A pardon can state that, for a period of time, a person has been without a recorded criminal offence and for the period of time his conduct was investigated by the National Parole Board he was of good conduct. Therefore, that person was pardoned for the offence which might have been an obstruction to his seeking employment. This provision will certainly have some effect on some of the situations which arise from time to time with regard to convicted persons. However, the real reform with respect to this matter cannot be accomplished by legislation.
I think the government should, as a matter of policy, further assist the people who find themselves in such a position. Even having granted them a pardon, they should provide sufficient funds to agencies such as the John Howard Society and the Elizabeth Fry Society. An officer of either of these organizations should accompany a convicted person to a prospective employer so that the whole circumstance can be discussed and assistance given to the applicant at this very critical moment.
I think this would be a very progressive step in rehabilitation. It might even take place sooner than the five years or two years, as the case may be. There is much more to be done in dealing with the treatment and rehabilitation of offenders. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that this Parliament considers this bill to be but one modest step in the progress to be made.

Perhaps I should put this particular suggestion on record, not because it is the law of the land but because the thought behind it may some day be the law of the land, and people should anticipate that this will be an issue in a few months' time in Parliament or in the committee. The proposal was as follows:
No person or firm furnishing information as to the financial credit rating of persons, or to employers as to the qualifications and suitability of their employees or prospective employees, or as to the qualifications and suitability of applicants for insurance or indemnity bonds shall furnish any information relating to the conviction of a person for an offence under an Act of the Parliament of Canada or a regulation made thereunder or disclose the fact of any such conviction at any time when the Board is authorized to make inquiries under subsection (2) of section 4 with respect to such person and in relation to that offence, unless the Minister certifies to the person or firm that proposes to furnish the information or disclose the fact of the conviction that no pardon in respect of the offence has been granted and that no application for such a pardon is under consideration.
As I reach the end of that mouth-breaking sentence, it becomes obvious that the minister or somebody in his department would have been up to his neck in detail writing to all the different credit companies. So, the proposal was probably unworkable in the form submitted.
The troika, if I may call the three of us that, tried to bring this change about, believing it is of importance that people should not be punished in a monetary way because of an offence for which they have served their time or otherwise paid their debt to society. They should not have a bad name hanging over them for the rest of their lives.
Another amendment was brought in making it an offence to violate any provision of the act, for example should somebody reveal that a person had a conviction for which he was subsequently pardoned. We tried to place as stiff a curtain about a person's past as possible in the circumstances.

Finally, there is the schedule which is set forth in the last page of the bill. It is of interest to note there was a long discussion in the committee as to whether the pardon should set forth the offences in respect of which the person was being pardoned or whether it should simply be in general terms. This gave us considerable difficulty; I do not think it is a matter on which it is very easy to make up one's mind. The consensus, as it turned out, was that the offences for which a pardon was being granted should be set forth specifically, I suppose for the very sensible reason that somebody might possibly get a general pardon and not disclose all the offences of which he or she had been guilty in the past.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I think this has been a classic example of, first, how a good committee can work very effectively, and second, how members can be united by the common bond of public interest even though they are separated by sharp political division. With these thoughts, may I say I think the measure before the House is an example of how well both these approaches have worked, and I commend it to the House for third reading.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very gratified that Bill C-5 has finally arrived at this stage. This concept of expunging a criminal record has had a long and varied history. A private member's bill was introduced in 1966 and went to the justice committee. There were various presentations to the committee which heard representatives from the John Howard Society, from the Magistrates Association and the Chiefs of Police Association. The committee recommended that the principle of expunging criminal records be endorsed, and the present government brought in the bill that is now before this House.
I should like to take this opportunity to congratulate all members of the justice committee. In particular, I should like to pay tribute to the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) and the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave). As these members have indicated on other occasions, this bill is a splendid example of how members from all parties can co-operate to produce a measure that I think will be for the benefit of all Canadians. I should also like to congratulate the Solicitor General (Mr. Mcll-raith). I must confess that I had certain reservations in connection with the bill, but we sat
May 12, 1970

down and discussed it and initiated amendments. As I have stated, I think we now have a good bill and I appreciate the co-operation shown.
We are ploughing a new field of legislation, and in this respect Canada is a pioneer. The main purpose of this bill is not to coddle criminals. It is simply an endeavour to help thousands of Canadians who in the past, perhaps through no fault of their own, have acquired a criminal record. This criminal record has hounded them for years and has created economic difficulties. We are now making an honest attempt to eliminate these difficulties as much as possible. We feel that the person who has served a term of imprisonment or paid a fine has discharged his debt to society, and that as far as possible he should be restored to his original civil status.
I believe that Professor Gough, professor of law at the University of Santa Clara, in an article in the Washington University Law Quarterly, very well summed up the purpose of this type of bill. I should like to quote his comments on page 149 of the Quarterly:
At the outset, it is necessary to limn with some particularity what expungement is and what it is not. By an expungement statute is meant a legislative provision for the eradication of a record of conviction or adjudication upon fulfilment of prescribed conditions, usually the successful discharge of the offender from probation and the passage of a period of time without further offence. It is not simply a lifting of disabilities attendant upon conviction and a restoration of civil rights, though this is a significant part of its effect. It is rather a redefinition of status, a process of erasing the legal event of conviction or adjudication, and thereby restoring to the regenerate offender his status quo ante.
Very briefly,-I think this point has been explained before- I should like to illustrate how the bill will work. An applicant will apply to the Solicitor General for a pardon. This application will be referred to the parole board. After proper investigation, if the parole board sees fit, the board will grant the applicant a certificate of pardon. I only hope that this proper investigation will in most cases be routine. By that, I mean that I do not think in many cases there should be a physical examination of the applicant in his home town, or wherever he may reside. I think in most cases it should be a scrutiny of the records filed. Based on that information, the pardon or certificate of good behaviour should be granted.
This certificate will aid the applicant in acquiring a visa. Perhaps it will also aid him in his employment. There is a further stipula-
Criminal Records
tion in the bill which provides, in effect, that all authorities over which the Canadian government has jurisdiction must not, once the record has been sealed, release it to the public. I think this is a most worth-while provision. Further, as has been mentioned before, if the record is the result of a summary conviction, the applicant can apply after two years. If the record is the result of an indictable offence, then the applicant must wait five years.
The main provision in the bill which, in my opinion, will assist those who are applying is the one that makes it mandatory for all government agencies that employ people not to ask the specific question: "Have you got a criminal record?" Instead they must ask a qualified question, such as: "Do you have a criminal record for which you do not have a pardon?", or something of that nature. This question is qualified and will enable the person who does not have a record, as well as the person who had one but who has been pardoned, to answer no. I think this is a most worth-while, indeed essential, provision.
This, of course, is not the final answer as far as helping people who have had criminal records is concerned. These people still have difficulty in obtaining a bond. The Solicitor General has taken a step in this direction by assisting certain agencies to provide bonds to those who have had criminal records. But I think we must go further and we should have a government bonding service to assist those people who have had criminal records in obtaining bonds.
In addition, provincial legislation in this field is required. This legislation applies only to those agencies over which the federal government has control. It will not apply to individual and corporate employers. I have talked to the attorney general of the province of Ontario, and the government of that province has shown some interest in this type of legislation. Again, I urge the Solicitor General to approach the attorneys general of the various provinces to see whether they would enact some type of complementary legislation.
Perhaps the greatest benefit that will flow from this statute is education. By that, I mean that it will show Canadians that our government is interested in the plight of the former offender; that it is willing to trust him; that the people of Canada want to accept him in the mainstream of society; that we believe it to be wrong and cruel to penalize an offender for life when he has already paid his debt to society.

May 12, 1970
Criminal Records
Professeur Gough well expounds the need for expungment of criminal records, and I should like to quote again his words as they appear at page 161 of the Quarterly:
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
If the offender is to be rehabilitated, two things must be done: he must be made a part of groups emphasizing values conducive to reform and law-abiding conduct, and he must concurrently be alienated from groups whose values are conducive to criminality. Neither of these goals is furthered by the failure of the law to provide means of restoring status.
In sum, there has been insufficient recognition of the responsibility of the penal law in alleviating the corrosive effects of the stigma its application necessarily creates. Dean Joseph Lohman of the University of California School of Criminology, a former sheriff of Cook County, Illinois, has written: "There is too little concern with the stigmatizing and alienating effect of arrests of such violators (minor offenders, especially first offenders). We equate them with bank robbers and murderers. Once a youngster has a police record, this fact, in the eyes of the law-and potential employers-is more real than the person himself. People stop looking at a young man. They look at his record, his "sheet" as it is called. Over and over boys told me, "It isn't me; it's the sheet. They won't listen to me." We have pushed these boys on the other side of the law. They may well stay there".
In a very real sense, the problem is one of the "self-fulfilling prophecy":	the offender initially moved toward reform becomes what we condemn him to be. The failure of the law to treat the former offender as a person with the potential to become a law-abiding and useful member of society, by omitting means of removing the infamy of his social standing, deprives him of an incentive to reform. To the extent that this shortcoming contributes to the repetition of criminal conduct, it renders the system of penal law a "monument to futility" and tends to erode public confidence in the legal order.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, again I congratulate the committee. I also congratulate the Solicitor General for introducing this bill. This is needed reform. It is forward-looking and will benefit many Canadians. I urge its speedy passage.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR RELIEF OF CONVICTED PERSONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to be allowed a few moments to speak about the criminal records bill. The legislation proposed by this government with respect to expunging criminal records after review and following a term of good behaviour is, in my opinion, one of the most humane and overdue changes ever to affect those who have erred against society. It will, if accepted, make Canada a leader in the treatment of a person who has committed a crime and who, to coin a phrase, has paid his debt. For having proposed this legislation, this government deserves the applause of all

those connected with the world of criminology. For having first brought this matter before the House in the form of a private member's bill, the present chairman of the Justice Committee, the respected member for Welland, (Mr. Tolmie) deserves special commendation. He has worked hard and long since June of 1966 to get this type of legislation passed.
Civilized mankind should be ever aware of the need for punishment of those members of our society who offend against it. Perhaps at this point in time, the twentieth century, it is our responsibility as members of civilized society to punish more severely than in the past those who are the authors of crime. Perhaps in this twentieth century more emphasis should be placed on the exemplary aspect of a penalty than on the punishment aspect. Perhaps penalties can serve a multitude of masters embracing punishment, example and correction. However, we are not here to debate punishments per se. I direct my remarks toward the permanent nature of those penalities meted out by our judiciary. Surely, we have matured beyond that line where we punish forever those who are guilty. Surely, as intelligent persons we are able to differentiate between punishment and vindictiveness. Surely, in this twentieth century of enlightenment and rapid advancement, we are not so savage that we condemn a man forever for an offence for which he already has paid his debt. I suggest that a criminal record, as recognized under our present legislation, does that exactly; that is, condemns him forever.
I recently had an experience with a man who, 50 years ago, went joy riding with a horse and buggy during a church service on a hot summer day. This man, then a boy, took another's horse and enjoyed the cool breeze rather than dutifully sitting through the sermon. The sermon was cut short because of the heat and the very irate owner was waiting for the lad when he returned to the front of the church. The boy was convicted and served nine months in jail for his transgression. Some 50 years later this man's daughters wanted him to join them in residence in the United States. Because of the existence of the criminal record, his only encounter with the law, the man was put to great trouble and much embarrassment, and all of this because of a joy ride on a hot summer day 50 years ago. This type of nonsense is the reason for the proposed change in the bill before us today.
The need for such change has been recognized for years, recommended and fought for
May 12, 1970

by the two most prominent jurists from our own Hamilton area. We perhaps are more indebted to such persons as His Honour Judge Walter Tuchtie of the criminal division of the provincial court at Hamilton and George Street, who I am delighted to see in the balcony today, the present chairman of the parole board, than we are aware. Both these gentlemen have painstakingly shown concern and desire over the years for such a program as our legislation now proposes. We, the people of Canada, owe them a debt of gratitude. A parole board empowered to review criminal records could well serve as the threshold. Records are reviewable. Under this bill, application can be made after a period of years to have the records expunged. The character of the offence, the behaviour of the holder and the tastes of the time as well as the other factors, well known to most members here, would be most meaningful in determining such a review. Records should be sealed, not destroyed. I do not stand here so naive as to suggest that the RCMP should not retain in its confidential files such relevant information as contained in a criminal record. But no employer, credit bureau or insurance company should enjoy this access except in exceptional circumstances.
Today, too often, citizens suffer because of some offence committed years ago, long after the penalty has been served and the person is completely rehabilitated. Often a credit report discloses, or an application form asks, about an old conviction and good citizens are embarrassed or a job lost or a bond turned down. This bill aims to prevent these unfair and cruel results by forbidding, once the record is sealed, this information from being disclosed or even requested. I hope, as the hon. member for Welland (Mr. Tolmie) mentioned, that the provincial governments will follow with appropriate legislation to close the remaining gaps. Our system of penalty should only prescribe that a convicted individual suffer punishment and pay his debt while confined to one of our federal or provincial institutions. Having paid his debt, sometimes in such archaic institutions as St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary which, in my opinion, should be closed down immediately, a man should be released. This release, to be meaningful, must be total.
A short while ago members of the Justice and Legal Affairs Committee inspected St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary at Montreal and I should like to make a comment about that at this time. I think, Mr. Speaker, we were all
Criminal Records
shocked at the conditions there, particularly in the psychiatric ward. In this ward were sick men kept in small, almost dark cells. The conditions were deplorable. We are keeping men in cells, not suitable even for animals. In my opinion, the staff was inadequate. We were told that there is a gradual phasing out of this penitentiary, but I urge the Solicitor General (Mr. Mcllraith) to accelerate the present plans which I understand call for the closing in two years' time. Since we visited there, I understand there have been two cases of suicide at this place and I hope that the present government will take immediate steps to remedy this situation.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I commend Bill C-5 to this House as one of the most progressive and humane in our time.

Mr. Speaker, you probably noticed a tendency to reminisce this afternoon because some of us feel that we have achieved part of our goal in this very important matter. I would say that in particular the hon. member for Welland (Mr. Tolmie) should be given full marks for the great efforts he has made in connection with this matter. I recall that in 1966 he introduced a private members bill with regard to expunging criminal records. The popular word at the time was "expunge". Expert witnesses appeared before the committee and we made a report. We received tremendous encouragement from the former solicitor general and a promise that legislation would come forth implementing some of the recommendations of the committee. That did not happen, and the former solicitor general was subsequently appointed to the Supreme Court of Ontario. Subsequently, the Ouimet Commission studied the matter of criminal records and came forth with an excellent report.
I will say right now that I want to commend the present Solicitor General (Mr. Mcllraith) for his fine efforts in connection with this bill. It so happened that when it came up for second reading I was away with a bad case of the flu, and I did not have the opportunity of participating in the debate. Later, at a committee meeting, I expressed my moral indignation by attempting to kick the Solicitor General in the shins for his approach to the matter because I felt that, even though we did not adopt the concept of expunction, I thought that probably we should pick up the idea expressed in the Ouimet Commission report with regard to annulment. The Solid-

May 12, 1970
Criminal Records
tor General had brought forth in his bill the idea of a pardon, indicating forgiveness. I was not satisfied with that approach at the time. I must say that at one time the Solicitor General indicated a rigidity and inflexibility with which I was not too happy, and other members of the committee felt likewise. Since then, however, he has shown an open-mindedness and an understanding with regard to this problem.
Again, I want to say that I am very happy that the Solicitor General is guiding this bill through the House. I am sure he would want me to say that some credit should be given to the chairman of the parole board for his assistance in this matter as well as to the deputy minister, Mr. Hollies, who showed a real appreciation of the problem. Even though at times he attempted to defend an unsupportable position, he showed the goodness and graciousness that a deputy minister can show at times. The result was that by setting up a troika of a representative from the Conservative party, a representative from the Liberal party and a representative from my party, we managed to formulate amendments which give this bill added strength. This is what is needed. The Solicitor General showed wisdom in accepting those amendments. Today, we have before us the bill for third reading. It will have a tremendous impact on many Canadians across Canada.
In the past, we treated criminals as a breed apart. Many Canadians said they deserved punishment and deserve to be branded as criminals for the rest of their lives. But in the last few years changes have taken place. Responsible and respectable citizens in Canada have been convicted of criminal offences, such as impaired driving. One can also recall fraud and bankruptcy offences being committed by responsible and respectable citizens within the community. In addition, many high school and university students have been convicted on drug charges. In the minds of many Canadians, the time has come when things must be corrected. I am sure that this bill is the result of the impact of convictions upon a particular section, the middle and the upper classes in our society. The greatest impact is upon the members of the poorer classes. It has been said many times that a criminal convinction has a very restrictive effect on a person's employment, a person's bonding and a person's freedom to travel. We have come forth with a bill which provides that after two years of good behaviour a person who has been convicted of a

summary offence can apply for a pardon, and after five years of good behaviour he may apply for a pardon in the case of an indictable offence.
I should like to say that the Ouimet Commission report was excellent, not only in the field of criminal records but in the total field of criminal law as well as the treatment of prisoners. One realizes that the members of the commission have gone into this subject in depth. They made a separation between summary and indictable offences, and their recommendation was that after two years the record of the former should be wiped out automatically, and after five years and a full hearing the record of the latter should be wiped out. We have not gone that far. When I reread the recommendations of the Ouimet Commission, I noted they said that, not only should the record be wiped out automatically after two years with regard to summary conviction but that as experience accumulated consideration should be given to broadening that category to include other offences.
Again, I must give the Solicitor General credit for undertaking to the committee members to review this legislation after a few years. I hope that after having experience with these applications we may again review this matter in depth, not only when the minister's estimates are before the House but also after two or three years.
An amendment has been proposed with regard to the cross-examination of witnesses, which again flows from the recommendations of the Ouimet Commission. The amendment provides that the cross-examination of a witness in any proceeding over which Parliament has jurisdiction concerning a previous conviction should have regard for the category of the conviction. Again we did not go that far in this bill, but we received an undertaking, not only from the Solicitor General but from the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner), that the Canada Evidence Act would be reviewed in depth and that probably the matter of cross-examination of witnesses concerning previous convictions will be studied either by the law reform commission or by some other committee established for this purpose. Therefore, the great troika within the committee and their supporting members withdrew their insistence with regard to this item.
Previous speakers have mentioned the results that will flow from this bill in the area of employment. All of us welcome what will follow, and I will not dwell on that now. It
May 12, 1970

has been said that many legal disabilities arising from a criminal record relate to property and civil rights, which fall within provincial jurisdiction. I urge the Solicitor General to take the initiative in arranging discussions between the federal government and the provincial governments with regard to rehabilitation in matters which fall under provincial control. I hope the Solicitor General will take the initiative with regard to employment and appointment forms, so that there may be uniformity across Canada. We can only achieve that uniformity through the initiative of the Solicitor General in asking the Attorneys General of the provinces to introduce complementary legislation in the provincial legislatures. Therefore, I am asking that he take the initiative in this important aspect. If he does not, he must know he will be on the carpet the next time he appears before the committee.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
The Solicitor General does not like strong criticism. He does like constructive criticism but, as I say, he does not like the strong, biting criticism that we at times tend to give him. I may say he will receive that criticism if he does not take an initiative in this field.
There is also the impediment with respect to travel in connection with criminal pardons. As the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Hogarth) pointed out, there are four different types of pardon, and the conditional pardon is the one usually granted by the Solicitor General on the advice or recommendation of the Chairman of the parole board. But now, we are going to shift the emphasis with regard to pardons. The Solicitor General knows that U.S. immigration authorities will not recognize a conditional pardon for immigration purposes. Therefore, I say he must again take the initiative to consult with U.S. authorities, and authorities in other countries, to reach agreement on international standards with regard to rehabilitation, without restrictions on travel between different countries being imposed on those granted pardons. Many young men who may hope to achieve pardons under this bill will encounter travel difficulties if the minister does not take the initiative to achieve agreement with U.S. and other authorities in respect of their pardons.
I see that the chairman of the parole board is in the gallery. I hope that he is swamped with so many applications for pardons that he will have to engage extra staff. In the past, there was a sort of limiting approach with regard to conditional pardons, and although a
Criminal Records
job has been done and probably a good job, there is a great deal of room for improvement. I think that he and his officials will exercise good judgment with regard to the type of investigations that will be necessary concerning the different offences that have been committed.
I recall a young fellow who had a long list of convictions, and who had rehabilitated himself. Now, he is married. He has a family, and is working steadily. He made an application on my initiative for a conditional pardon. One day he was having lunch with his foreman when a person came in and asked to speak to the foreman in private. It so happened that it was about the fellow with whom the foreman was having lunch. He got assurance from the foreman that this young man had rehabilitated himself, was steadily employed, and was accepting his responsibilities in the community. The good feature of it all was that the young man had told his employer about his convictions, and so the foreman was prepared for the inquiry.
A judicious, neat approach is required in these matters so that an investigation may not upset the good relations existing between an applicant and his employer. I hope the chairman of the parole board will instruct his men, when they make investigations, to do so with all cleverness and quietness.
I wish to say one final word concerning the form of a pardon. The conditional pardon granted today lists the convictions of the person concerned, and then in archaic but humble language says that the person is forgiven with regard to these offences. I and other hon. members attempted to have this form changed in the committee. We felt that the list of convictions should not appear in the pardon. If a man had established good behaviour over a period, we felt he should be given a certificate worthy of showing not only to his own family but to his employer and others. If we list his convictions we may be destroying the full effect of his pardon. I hope that the Solicitor General and the chairman of the parole board will devise a pardon form that an applicant may show freely to his family, his employer, and other members of the community. One would not want the pardon in the form of a B.A. degree or M.A. degree from a university. One would not want it given in that type of language, but rather in the type of language whereby we as a community say to the applicant, "We know you made a mistake in the past. We know

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to see the changes that are made in Bill C-5. I hasten to say I am in favour of the principle of the bill, but there are one or two points I wish to put before the House. I am a little bit confused about how you can give a person a conditional pardon. To me, a pardon is either a pardon or it is not.
There are some cases in which a man could not expect to receive a pardon. As broadminded as I am, and I consider myself very broadminded and forward-looking, there is no such thing as paying your debt to society for certain offences. I shall refer to only one or two. Take the case of a serious sex offence against a child. No term of imprisonment, no punishment with a whip, no fine can turn back the pages of time and restore that child to its physical and mental health. There is no question of whether he has paid his debt to society, it cannot be done.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
On the other hand, I rule out revenge. Because some weak minded individual or some sadistic and cruel person perpetrates such an offence, is no reason why society should stoop to his level. He must be segregated for a period of time to try to find the reason for his action. He must be given the opportunity to have the medical attention which is often necessary in such cases, and he must be offered the understanding of people trained in social work. We hope all this will help rehabilitate him. If he has committed an offence like this, society owes him nothing except the humanitarian attempt to rehabilitate him.
I do not think that five years is long enough to completely expunge the record in such cases. If you do that, or give him a certificate of merit, it is quite possible that he might seek employment at one of our institutions which care for the mentally ill. He might even get preferred treatment unless it were made very plain that a person who has been found guilty of this type of offence is unemployable under some circumstances. It is not society's fault that he has done this thing. It is not society's fault that the record cannot 
be completely expunged. It is not society's fault that he has put himself in a position where he is no longer to be trusted with the care of the very young, the old, or the mentally weak, of people who have no protection against him. In such circumstances, it might be a case of a child's word against his or that of a person who is mentally deficient or very old. I do not intend to go into case histories this afternoon but they are well known.
The second type of offence which I think should rarely, if ever, be removed from the record is an offence against our country. A man who is guilty of treason-I do not mean treason against the person of the Queen necessarily, but treason against the right of free democracy in Canada-should not get a pardon after five years of good behaviour in my opinion.
Of course, I know that within this act there is that protection. Nevertheless, Clause 5(b) of Bill C-5 reads in part:
-unless the pardon is subsequently revoked, vacates the conviction in respect of which it is granted and, without restricting the generality of the foregoing, removes any disqualification to which the person so convicted is, by reason of such conviction, subject by virtue of any act of the Parliament-
I am thinking in particular of hiring for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. If a man has been guilty of treason against Canada, I do not think five years or any period of time would make him a fit person to be entrusted with the security of our country. If we cannot trust the commissioner of the mounted police and those who work under him, we cannot trust anybody.
Though I agree with the general spirit of this bill, perhaps a subclause should be added somewhere to the effect "except in such cases where the said statute is directly aimed at protecting the security of Canada." You can read that into the subsequent clauses of the bill but it is not there in black and white. One would gather from reading clause 5 that nobody was to be disqualified from being hired for any job in Canada, providing he had five years of good behaviour and had satisfied the board of this fact.
I am glad that the bill has been amended so that we draw distinctions between summary conviction cases and indictable offences. Of course, unless you are guilty of an indictable offence you do not go to jail for the periods of time which would qualify you for the more serious sections in this bill. I think we should have a paragraph which spells out those very
May 12, 1970

Criminal Records
few cases where you cannot pay your debt to society, where you cannot rehabilitate yourself to the level of a person who has never been guilty of a serious offence.
We need a little flexibility and I see it here in the bill. I should not like to see the bill so rigid that it demands that the board accept people in positions relating to security or the care of the young, the weak or the mentally crippled. There is a great need for a man with a criminal record to be employed, but I doubt very much whether a certificate stating that he has been rehabilitated would do him any good. I think there should be changes in the law. Perhaps we should enact statutes to the effect that a man may not be deprived of employment when his crime has been strictly against property, such as theft, borrowing a bicycle, infringements of the traffic act or the liquor act.
Perhaps even those people who try marijuana and who are convicted under the Narcotic Control Act should be treated in an entirely different way from those desperate and unspeakable criminals who destroy the bodies and souls of our young people for their own aggrandizement. I would have no hesitation in writing into the bill the broadest acceptance of the experimental quality of youth, and the fact that they can rehabilitate themselves very rapidly. However, the drug pusher, the importer and those who enable them to carry on their trade, should not have their records expunged after five years of good behaviour. I cannot be convinced that after this short time they should be able to qualify for positions in charge of young people or, say, for employment with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to train the preventive service squad.
The protection of the public must remain our paramount concern, no matter how forward-looking we might regard ourselves, or how progressive. Rehabilitation must always stand ahead of revenge. There is no place in Canadian society for revenge. You are listening to a man who knows, having spent 25 years of public service in the police force. I have never seen Canadian society edging forward one inch towards being brutal. It is not given to revenge, nor even to self-righteousness. The protection of the public is another matter, however, and I know the board will do its best to protect Canada. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I have the distinction of being just about the only non-lawyer who is interested in this matter and, therefore, I will probably not agree with many of the things which have been said. This is a lawyer's piece of legislation and its results in years to come may remind people of the sort of thing which happened yesterday. Someone who has been convicted at 17 years of age of possessing marijuana may find five years later when looking for a job that he faces great difficulty, even if he has tried to erase the stigma of the conviction.
The hon. member speaking before me was talking about the hardened criminal who wears his convictions as a badge, finds them of advantage, and secures criminal employment on the strength of them. I am not speaking of people like that; I am speaking of young people who have been convicted in their youth and in later years find it is a very serious matter.
The legislation before us contains nothing new. We already have parole provisions. I can remember a young lad who was convicted of a matter involving a calf. There was some question about the calf's parentage. At long last the police agreed that he was probably innocent of that charge but guilty of the two or three charges that had been dropped. After a lot of trouble, it was decided to pardon the lad. He said "I don't want your pardon because I was not guilty in the first place". Clearly, pardons have been kicking around for a long time.
It seems to me that in the last few days several pieces of legislation have been introduced by private members that were 100 per cent better than legislation which was introduced after a committee had held great discussions on it. The legislation, suggested by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. Tolmie), who originally proposed this idea, was good. The present legislation before us is not worth a damn. If you want to expunge criminal records in the way suggested by this bill, then I say this bill is not really of any value. When the hon. member for Welland talked about expunging records, he meant what he said. He wanted criminal records to disappear. In the province of Ontario, if I am convicted of speeding, I lose three points. If I make a turn

May 12, 1970
Criminal Records
without giving proper signals, I lose another three. But, Mr. Speaker, after a time, if I behave myself while driving my car, those points are returned to me.
The Solicitor General (Mr. Mcllraith) has been around long enough to know that if he wishes to do anything worth while in this field, he must expunge convictions. If you have paid the penalty that the law demands, you should not have to go on paying forever. If the province of Ontario did not return to a driver the points he loses, eventually it would mean that drivers would either have to be allowed a loss of five or seven points a year, or else no one would possess a driving licence.
I am sure the hon. member for Welland was thinking of individual cases in which young people have done something bad, been punished, and later sought to remove the stigma of the conviction. As a non-lawyer, I suggest that the last place in the world to place the burden in this matter is with the National Parole Board. Let me illustrate what will happen if you seek a pardon. Let us say that I was convicted of bank robbery when I was 18 years old. Nobody knows about this now. I live in another community. I have been living properly, working hard and have given up my profession of robbing banks. Let us say a number of years have gone by. No one knows I have been in jail-I have a healthy tan now-and I go to the parole board for a pardon. And what does that body do? Immediately it gets in touch with people who are involved with credit ratings and tries to find out about my financial situation. The board will then write to the police in the community and will say such and such a man was convicted ten or 15 years ago in such and such an area of robbing a bank; would you check around and see if he has been in trouble in your area. The board would make all kinds of inquiries.
Finally, it would send me a nice piece of paper saying, "You robbed a bank in such and such a year, but you have not robbed another, and to prove this you may show people this piece of paper." That is what this measure boils down to. That reminds me of the guy who came out of the insane asylum. He told people who said he was a little odd, "I am not crazy; maybe the rest of you are crazy, but I am not because I have a piece of paper proving I am not crazy, and it is from a mental institution." That is just about the

kind of thing that will happen if the parole board is involved in the rating of pardons.

I believe in this bill. I also believe in the amendment which was made in committee which would maintain the observance of the holiday of July 1, except when it falls upon a

speechtext:
I will not forget the Fathers of Confederation. I respect them. But I am thinking of the Canada that we are discussing in this bill. In this regard, what province has recently shown more life, more spirit, and more desire to have its citizens remain Canadians than the great province of Quebec? All of us in Canada salute our brothers and sisters in Quebec for their very definite decision, made only two weeks ago, to remain part of this country and to play their part in the nation's life, as they have in the past. They have provided a shining example and pointed the way for the rest of us to follow if we are best to serve our country. All hon. members who share the same viewpoint as the majority of the people of the province of Quebec will support the bill that is presently before us.
Some may wonder why I, coming from a heavily Anglicized constituency like Brant, Ontario, have consented to present this bill.

May 12, 1970
Canada Day
In addition to the people of Quebec, who want one Canada, there are those people who came to this country during the last century from various countries in Europe and have chosen Canada to be their home. In the county of Brant, which I have the honour to represent in this House, there are large numbers of such people. To itemize but a few of them, we have people of German descent, of Polish descent, of Italian descent, of Hungarian descent, of Ukrainian descent and Dutch descent. All of them love this country. I say most decidedly that I have not forgotten these people who have shown loyalty, devotion and dedication to this country and to its future. They have expressed themselves to me in large numbers as supporting the bill that is presently before the House. The word "Canada" being an Indian name, my Six Nations constituents, original Canadians, must be elated at the suggestion that July 1 be renamed "Canada Day". The word "Canada" is taken from their language, their own background and traditions.
Canada is not directed today by a dead hand. Sir Samuel Leonard Tilley was a great man in his day, but we are shortly to enter the last quarter of the 20th century, and I would ask whether we are going to have our future perhaps curtailed or abridged by 19th century solecisms or by sources who know not the Canada of today. Even at the time of confederation Sir John Macdonald would, in my view, have jettisoned the word "dominion" quickly had his chief collaborator, Sir Georges Etienne Cartier, tipped him off, as it were, that he could not get away with it.
Since this is a private member's bill, let us not permit it to be made a government bill if we can possibly prevent it. I believe, as I have always believed, in Parliament as an institution. Therefore, let us demonstrate that private Members of Parliament have as much impact today on the life of the nation as one might be led to expect in an ideal Parliament.

Well, Mr. Speaker, let us all walk together towards the glorious future that awaits our beloved country.

speakeroldname: Mr. A. D. Alkenfcrack (Fxonienac-Lennox and Addington):
