speechtext:
various terms wherever reference is made to "Dominion Day." It is interesting to note that the sponsor of the bill and the movers of the amendments all bear names of Anglo-Saxon origin. Why is this? We of other origins do not wish the name of our national holiday to be changed; neither do the majority of the people of Anglo-Saxon origin. "Dominion" is the very title of our country. For those who might be resentful of a suggestion that we are a British dominion, I say that this country never was a British dominion in a civic or corporate sense. It was originally, in its infancy, a French colony. After 1759 it became a British colony as a result of circumstances beyond our control, and in 1867 it became a self-governing country with equal opportunity for everyone under the British Crown.
To those members of the House who associate the word "Dominion" with domination by Britain, I say this is a misconception. In fact, there is more attempt at our domination today by other foreign countries. Britain, the founder of responsible government and the mother of our system of government, is far too discreet to attempt domination.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO SUBSTITUTE "CANADA" FOR "DOMINION"
speechtext: She is the mother of freedom.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO SUBSTITUTE "CANADA" FOR "DOMINION"
speechtext:
Britain has never dominated this country in the way some people indicate. The child, Canada, is now a man: all domination died with the end of the First Great War and the passing of the Statute of Westminster. We 21 million Canadians dominate the northern half of the North American continent. This country is a confederation of ten provinces, the Yukon and the Northwest Territories, each a vast dominion in its own boundaries, each fearless and free in directing and electing its own destiny. All at the same time are linked together by one dominion government. This government possesses all the necessary powers to deal with our 3J million square miles of dominion territory and to deal with the rest of the world.
Let us continue to be known as the Dominion of Canada. I say to the people, "You have found it good; do not abandon it". The name "Dominion Day", moreover, is much more pleasing to the ear than "Confederation Day" or other names. It is alliterative and euphonious. We note with pride that the Fathers of Confederation drew considerable inspiration from spiritual sources and insisted on something that would mark the new and higher status of the federation of the four original provinces. They took from Psalm 72 the biblical quotation, "He shall have dominion from
Canada Day
sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth". These words were suggested by Sir Leonard Tilley, later governor of New Brunswick and, I have heard on good grounds, in the presence of the Hon. George Brown, the ancestor of the member who has placed this bill before us. "Dominion" has nothing whatever to do with the domination of this country, nor any of the citizens of the Dominion of Canada.
If we should change this wonderful name we would have to put the stone-masons to work around this building obliterating the word "Dominion". The east side of the Peace Tower has the inscription I just quoted, and "dominion from sea to sea" inscribed on one of its sturdy arches. There is evidence of this identification all across the country in cities, towns and municipalities other than the capital. The Privy Council chamber in the east block houses a tremendous mural map on the south wall entitled, "The Dominion of Canada, 1886". What a tradition this name "Dominion of Canada" bears! Every Canadian, as had the Fathers of Confederation, has great spiritual resources available to him. Our patriotism emanates from and has its source not only in ourselves and our relationships with our fellow citizens but also in the majesty of nature and the physical grandeur and beauty of our great dominion from the misty Grand Banks of Newfoundland to the Rocky Mountains and Vancouver and Queen Charlotte Islands.
The whole problem involved in this debate arises from a semantic misunderstanding on the part of the mover and those who have presented amendments to the bill. To prove this point I should like to bring to the attention of hon. members an editorial from the Kingston Whig Standard of Friday, May 1, 1970. It is entitled, "A Dominion it is". The article states in part.
Canada will gain nothing but derision from those -both at home and abroad-who happen to know her history, if this change in the name of our most significant national holiday is made. It won't bring the country down in ruins. But it will destroy a proud and resounding national designation-"The Dominion of Canada"-and it will also prove Canadians to be the most callow of adolescents when it comes to appreciating their own heritage.
It is quite a lengthy editorial, Mr. Speaker, and that is all I shall quote for the record. I submit that those who would like to see Bill C-29 pass do not appreciate or understand their own heritage.
I shall close by placing on the record "A Song of Canada". This is a poem written

by one of our now deceased Canadian citizens, that great Scottish-Canadian poet Robert Reid. Many members may remember this poem from their schooldays. I am proud to place it on the record because it best describes the love we should bear for our country, its sublime beauty, principles and origins. Written in 1910, the poem is as follows:
Sing me a song of the great Dominion!
Soul-felt words for a patriot's ear!
Ring out boldly the well-turned measure.
Voicing your notes that the world may hear;
Here is no starveling-Heaven forsaken- Shrinking aside where the Nations throng;
Proud as the proudest moves she among them- Worthy is she of a noble song!

Baring their brows in the dazzling blue;

Emblems of all that is grand and true;
Free as the eagles around them soaring;
Fair as they rose from their Maker's hand;

The white-topp'd peaks of our mountain land!

Here, if at all, man's soul might quail:

Sing me the joy of her fertile prairies.
League upon league of the golden grain:
Comfort, housed in the smiling homestead

Plenty, throned on the lumbering wain.
Land of contentment! May no strife vex you, Never war's flag on your plains unfurl'd;
Only the blessings of mankind reach you- Finding the food for a hungry world!
Sing me the charm of her blazing camp-fires; Sing me the quiet of her happy homes,
Whether afar 'neath the forest arches Or in the shade of the city's domes;
Sing me her life, her loves, her labors:
All of a mother a son would hear;
For when a lov'd one's praise is sounding Sweet are the strains to the lover's ear...

Sing me the song, then; sing it bravely:
Put your soul in the words you sing;
Sing me the praise of this-
-great Dominion-
Clear on the ear let the deep notes ring.
[Mr. Alkenbrack.J
Here is no starveling, Heaven forsaken, Crouching apart where the nations throng;
Proud as the proudest moves she among them; Well is she worthy a noble song!
I am sure all members will agree that a Dominion it is, so a Dominion let it remain.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that private members' hour has almost concluded and that other hon. members obviously wish to speak, I propose to confine my remarks to a few sentences only.
The name of our country is described in the first operative section of the British North America Act as being "One Dominion under the name of Canada." From the very beginning of this country "Dominion" has been association by law and by tradition with our national holiday. The norm "Dominion" is in the minds of a large number of our fellow citizens associated traditionally, historically and emotionally with "Canada." It is the official name of this country. It therefore seems to me appropriate that it should continue to be the description given to our national holiday.
We Members of Parliament who are dealing with a matter which commands what we call a free vote of this House are forced to realize our extreme power as legislators. We have it within our power today to change the name of our national holiday and, indirectly, to change the title and style of our country. It is my opinion that as legislators we should exercise our power with prudence and with proper respect for the views of our fellow citizens.
I do not know what other hon. nembers have done, but when this proposal was first made in the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs of which I was a member, before the Easter recess I asked that consideration of this question be held over so that all of us would be able to consult our constituents and determine their views. I took every means within my power to ask the people in my constituency what they thought of a proposal to change the name "Dominion Day" to "Canada Day." I received 198 letters, 181 of which were completely opposed to changing the present title of "Dominion Day." Fifteen letters approved "Canada Day," and two constituents suggested the title "Confederation Day."
I think many people would say that when changes are proposed, those who are in opposition are more likely to express themselves

This constituency is in truth one of the oldest parts of Canada. It was to this area that the United Empire Loyalists first came. It is one of the oldest parts of English-speaking Canada, and I contend that the views of the people whom I represent deserve respect and attention. I hope that the House will accord it to them.
I also suggest to all hon. members that we must in this House exercise our great powers with prudence and with proper respect for the views of all our people, as 1 said at the beginning. We have held our country together by being very respectful of the views of minorities, be they linguistic, regional, economic or religious. Throughout our history we have endeavoured to avoid making decisions which are divisive, particularly when they relate to the deeply-held convictions of people in Canada.
At this critical time in our history I would hate our country to be divided by an acrimonious debate about the name of its national holiday. Any change in the name of our national holiday should unite, and not divide us. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before five o'clock we were discussing Bill C-5 which provides for the relief of persons who have been convicted of offences and have subsequently rehabilitated themselves. I was mentioning that this bill, not being all it should be, will ultimately bring about a situation such as developed in the House yesterday. Hon. members will remember that some time ago when the amendments to the Criminal Code were being considered, one of the amendments related to abortion.
Everyone who was involved with the legislation, knew that far from being beneficial, the amendment would be restrictive. Before the law was changed, if a doctor wanted to perform an abortion he would, knowing that he was about to undertake something on the edge of legality, make his decision in conjunction with another doctor. Now the law says that there must be a therapeutic abortion committee. But only large hospitals can set up therapeutic abortion committees-so that far from being beneficial, that amendment to the Criminal Code has proved to be restrictive.
What bothers me is that although there was a lot of hullabaloo about the abortion provision, and although many people thought we were taking a forward step in this field, we were not. Quite understandably, many people were frustrated when nothing concrete happened after all that talk. The other day we witnessed a demonstration on behalf of young, pregnant girls who were looking for relief in the law on abortion. Anticipating that legislation passed by this parliament would bring them relief, they were disappointed to find that it would not.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
The young people today are engaging in activities that in many cases are anti-social. They are the kind of activities that bring the young people into conflict with society as we know it. In many cases they will get themselves into great difficulty. Because of the newspaper coverage of this debate, their opinion will be that their offence will not be known: they will think they will be able to get rid of the stigma attached to the offence. They expect to be able to say to a prospective employer, legally and without danger of conflict, "No, I have not been convicted of a criminal offence''. That will not be true. Even if they receive a pardon, the people in their community will still know about the original offence. They will be aware that this person

When the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, the hon. member for Welland (Mr. Tolmie), initially-brought this matter before Parliament, hon. members will recall that a member of this House had in his youth been convicted of a criminal offence. There was an attempted blackmail. The hon. member stated that in fact he had been convicted and the blackmail attempt was unsuccessful. When the hon. member drafted his private member's bill asking for the expunging of records, that is exactly what he meant. That is what should happen.
Most members of the committee could quite easily be appointed to the Supreme Court. It is certainly a lawyers' club that is operating in that committee. They operate at a very high legal level, not at the level of the average person. They deal in legalities, technicalities, precedents and all the hocus-pocus that belongs in the Supreme Court.

And justice. There is no argument about that. However, it is confusing. People practising law are honourable: they are doing an excellent job. Appearing before that committee are representatives of the police and the parole board. These people have a selfish and involved interest. This high-paid help advises the committee how to operate so that society will be protected.
There is nothing in this bill that could not have been done previously. If I am wrong, I ask the minister to tell me. To the best of my knowledge, a person could always petition for pardon of a conviction: it is not necessary to wait five years. It is possible to petition to the Queen for a pardon. Although the pardon is not always granted, there is the right to apply. All this bill does is state that a person can apply in a certain way and the machinery will be set up to make the pardon possible. An investigation is made to see whether the person has been living a good, clean life for the past five years, and if so the pardon will be granted.
Thousands of people in this country are waiting for this kind of legislation. They believe that Parliament has decided that if a person behaves himself for a reasonable period of time his criminal record will be expunged. If we were honest we would state in this bill that no employer has the right to
[Mr. Peters.l
ask any employee if he has a criminal record or if he is a Jew or a Protestant. In most areas this question cannot be asked. We are promising those who have a criminal record that their good name can be restored by being granted a pardon. That is not what the public wants. It is not what we promised them. It is certainly not what the hon. member had in mind when he introduced this question several years ago in a private member's bill.
Hon. members should carefully consider the legal arguments being presented. I think most members will agree that a criminal record should automatically be eliminated after a certain period of time. I have used the example of a driver's licence. A person is permitted so many points. If he loses those points, after a certain period of time they are automatically given back to him. He does not have to apply for them. Surely the Department of Justice could review convictions in a similar manner. If a person is convicted in his youth of attempted armed robbery, stealing an automobile, joy-riding or a misdemeanour under the Highway Traffic Act, that information would be listed with the Department of Justice. It would be available to the provincial police, the federal police and very likely Interpol. It would be well known in the community where the conviction was registered. There would be no problem in automatically eliminating records where there had been no conviction in the previous five years. I think this would be fair. When a person serves a sentence and has met the requirements of the law, the penalty should not continue forever. It is our responsibility to expunge the criminal record. It should not be the responsibility of the individual to ask to have his record cleared, because it will not happen; the police will not forfeit the record. A prospective employer should not ask for information concerning a conviction more than five years old. The record should no longer exist. When applying for a job, a person should not be asked about a criminal record any more than he should be asked about his religion or nationality. It is of no interest, and should not bar him from obtaining employment.
I received recently a letter from someone who was convicted when he was young. He wanted to know whether he could obtain a passport. I was surprised to learn that the government did not care about his previous conviction. That question is not asked when applying for a passport. I understand the question is not asked when applying for a

When I read this bill I am reminded of the story which most members here have read. It was 20 years ago that I read "Les Miserables" by Victor Hugo. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that having been exonerated after serving in the galleys, Jean Valjean received a yellow passport, or paper, on which it was stated:
Jean Valjean, a liberated convict, having been convicted for buglary (five years) and attempted escape (14 years) and having served 19 years is hereby freed.
You will recall that he went from one end of France to the other, and every time he showed that paper it proved to be his death-knell. Why? Because this is the nature of the beast; this is the nature of human beings. The intention is good, but intentions sometimes pave the road to heartbreak.

What shall we do? We recognize that vengeance is not the purpose of society. We are not the first to do so. Two thousand years ago an attempt was made to recognize this evil in mankind, this desire of men to improve their position at the expense of others. Now we have reached a stage at which we are civilized enough not to wish to punish a man over and over again, not to incarcerate him repeatedly, if not behind bars then by our actions. We seem to overlook, when we introduce law reform, that we are human beings, not a band of angels. Human beings, unlike other animals, love to be cruel, to some extent, and they are aggressive and vengeful. No other creature on earth is as vengeful as man. That is a matter of practicality.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
Now, let us suppose that this bill is passed. Let us also suppose that a man applies for a pardon, though I gather from the hon. member v/ho has just spoken that very few men will apply because by applying you bring more old skeletons out of the closet than if you do not apply. When a pardon is granted, what will be the situation? Mankind is curious, and gossip will condemn the man whether or not he has had a pardon. The minute his employer hears that the man had a conviction, pardon or no he will be leery of

him. Again, that is a practical matter. His neighbours will talk the minute they know; his family will suffer and he will have to

For all practical purposes, the intent of the bill is spelled out in clause 5 in wonderful language. It reads:
The grant of a pardon
(a) is evidence of the fact that the Board, after making proper inquiries, was satisfied that an applicant was of good behaviour and that the conviction in respect of which the pardon is granted should no longer reflect adversely on his character-
Very noble language! Many times I have heard him express the same apprehensions that have been expressed by others in the House.
To think that society would accept a stronger measure than this is to dream, instead of to face reality. Let us suppose that all the suggestions made by the hon. member opposite had been incorporated in the bill. If a record were expunged, does he not think for one moment that clever entrepreneurs would seek out such record? For a certain fee, employers could be given the exact particulars of any record. I would ask the hon. member what he would do about that. Would the hon. gentleman suggest that the newspapers should not be allowed to print the details of trials, convictions and the names of those concerned? Or would he consider this a restriction on the freedom of the press? If he does, then it does not matter what this bill provides. Mr. Speaker, since I am speeding along here, I should like to continue. I promised the minister that I would not take more than five minutes, and I intend to keep my promise. I should like to make a suggestion. Clause 6 (2) of the bill provides:
-no such record shall be disclosed to any person, nor shall the existence of the record or the fact of the conviction be disclosed to any person-
I suggest that if there were added to that the words "or by any person" we would achieve the practical solution. In other words, if we made it illegal for one person to disclose to another the criminal record of a person who had been granted a pardon, the result would be a practical one: the newspapers would go through their morgue and blot out the names so that no one would be identified. I would also suggest the further provision that anyone who disclosed the past criminal conviction of a person who had obtained a pardon would be liable for damages. I see no reason why that could not be done. Certainly I think my suggestions would accomplish a great deal more than the suggestions made by the hon. member opposite.
There is nothing in business that entrepreneurs dislike more than the possibility of having to pay money in the form of damages. You cannot very well decree that newspapers do not cover trials and publish names, although in today's context I do not see why it is necessary to publish culprits' names. Nevertheless, I do not think the freedom of the press would be restricted to any great extent if the press were not allowed to publish names. Does it really have to be publicized that it was Tom Jones or Jack Smith who was convicted of burglary? In former times, when citizens had no other protection, this might have been important, but not today. But as long as the law is as it is, we should make sure that if a person tells another person that a third party has been convicted, and as a result that third party suffers damage, such person should be liable for damages. That is the only way to put a stop to this practice.

Mr. Speaker, I was not a member of the committee that considered this bill. However, I do have the personal experience of a constituent on this topic. I have listened to some of the arguments expressed tonight and feel I should add this personal experience to our deliberations. I have no desire to get in the minister's hair on this subject, if that were in any way possible. But I have a strong feeling about a person who has been convicted of a crime, who has served his time and paid his debt to society through his period of incarceration. As the hon. member across the way has said, I do not think there is any point in perpetuating vengeance or punishment. But what happens in fact is exactly that-a person who has made one slip or false move, perhaps very early in life, is forced to carry the stigma for the rest of his life no matter how he has since conducted himself.
My personal experience has relation to a person convicted of extortion some 35 years ago. This example relates to the minister's department. The person concerned applied for a job associated with the Department of Justice. When asked whether he had a criminal record, he said he had not. The truth is that he lied. This man, in his late sixties, was forced to lie because he had only Hobson's choice: he had the choice of lying and not getting the job, or of telling the truth and not getting the job.
A person who has a criminal record carries it to his grave. Of course, under this legislation there could be a pardon if the person

Criminal Records
should apply for a pardon. However, I do not think that a person who has for 35 years lived as a good citizen should have to go through the routine of applying for a pardon. Also, I do not believe it is fair to hold out the hope to individuals with criminal records that their records will be expunged when this is not really the case. The record is there, and will remain there. But this bill says, "We will forgive you".
The criminal record of a person is forced to still remain. I believe that on third reading of a bill such as this there is a kind of hope that criminal records will be forgotten. But I wonder if that actually will be the case. I suppose there are people who have greater hopes than me that legislation of the type we have before us will solve the problem. I do not believe it will. I think the same kind of sinister name and record which a person with a conviction has will remain with him regardless of this legislation. Therefore, in a sense we are holding out hope of a type that really does not exist.
I add my voice to that of people who feel that once a person has served his sentence and has lived up to the expectations of the community, his case automatically should come up for review by the Department of Justice or the Department of the Solicitor General, and automatically his offence against society-for which he has paid dearly- should be expunged.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this bill is an important part of the attempt to improve the whole corrections program of this country. It is an integral part of the total program and should be viewed as such. subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR RELIEF OF CONVICTED PERSONS
speechtext:
This particular facet of the corrections program is an attempt, as part of the major changes being made, to provide a practical measure that will assist those persons who have been convicted of having committed a crime and have since rehabilitated themselves. This measure should help them avoid having to suffer the unjust conse-

quences of having been convicted. It is, as I said, part of a larger program that we have been carrying out within the past year. We have sharply increased the size of the National Parole Board. We have increased its scope of work by sending panels of the board into our penal institutions to interview the prisoners there.
We have been able to obtain information from the inmates concerning the desirability of applying for parole. This was not true as recently as two years ago. We have sought to make sharp changes in retraining programs in the institutions. This is a difficult task, but as hon. nembers will appreciate substantial changes have been made in the physical characteristics of the buildings. The number of institutions has increased from 9 to 34 in the last 8 years, while there has not been a very large increase in the number of inmates. There has also been a change in the training program. Perhaps I could pick out an example to illustrate the point I wish to make. Instead of following what had been the practice for many years, that of giving some trade training in certain areas-some of which, I regret to say, has fallen into disuse-we have made changes in an effort to provide training in those areas that would lead to employment on release.
This change can best be illustrated by the rather well-publicized program of having firms engaged in a certain field provide training. This has been done in respect of computer programming. There has been work in that new field of activity. It is interesting to note that the small group in the first graduating class all had jobs available before they were released. I have picked out that one program merely for purposes of illustration. There are others. We are trying to develop and press this program forward rapidly, because it is quite clear to anyone who studies the whole situation carefully that just as 10 years ago the thrust properly was put on changing and improving the accommodation, if you like to call it that, for inmates, the thrust in the next 10 years has moved away from that aspect into the treatment and rehabilitation of the individual person who is unfortunate enough to be an inmate. We have also made other changes which I could mention in providing for supervision during the period of statutory remission of persons released before the expiry of the full term for which they were sentenced during the statutory periods.
May 12, 1970

[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
With reference to this particular measure, it is quite clear that there have been unfair and unjust consequences persisting throughout the lives of men who have been convicted of an offence which they had committed earlier in their lives. In an effort to remove the unjust situation attaching to these individuals we have attempted to do what we can. One of the things we have been doing is to have more and more of the community groups working with the parole board or penitentiary service, as the case may be, in addition to the work we do for the inmates directly and immediately. We have been getting a better receptivity in the minds of the community at large because in the final analysis the acceptance of that concept will correct all these unjust situations, not legislation by itself.
We also started in anticipation, because the processes are lengthy, to try to use the existing legislation for pardons more extensively than we have. While that did not affect many persons, it did provide an opportunity to acquire much experience in the method of removing the consequences of convictions on persons who have been rehabilitated. Certain things were found out about that. We then studied the private member's bill, to which I think all members of the House acknowledge a debt of gratitude because it brought forward this subject a few years ago in another Parliament.

-for the method of dealing with the subject. We came to the conclusion that the best approach was to provide a document that would indicate to the community at large and to the prospective employers, where the matter arose, that these people had rehabilitated themselves. It became rather clear, to the extent to which we can get information on the subject, that persons who had criminal records desired this distinction themselves, although there is no proof for that statement in any statistical way because, as hon. members will know, it is difficult to obtain precise information on it. But it is clear in the minds of most who have worked in this field that it is desirable to draw a distinction between those persons who had earlier convictions and who have regrettably continued their criminal activities-and regrettably there are some such persons-and those who have succeeded in rehabilitating themselves.
So the concept is to grant pardon, and when pardon has been granted to get all the records and have them sealed where they cannot be obtained by anyone except in the limited circumstances set out in the bill, with all the precautions, because occasionally there can conceivably be circumstances where it might be desirable in the interest of the state and society at large to obtain them again. There is no legislation on this subject on which we can base ourselves. It is a matter of going forward into a new field. We believe this will work. I know of the tremendous change in attitude on this whole subject that has taken place among employers, mainly in the corporation field. a new concept, and is a significant change worthy of note and commendation here.
The bill has other technical details upon which I do not need to elaborate. But I want to emphasize that there is every reason to expect that this bill will be of tremendous help to a large number of persons who have had convictions and who have long since reentered society in a normal way and rehabilitated themselves fully, but still suffer the consequences of an earlier conviction. It is the best possible method we could devise to meet the problem in a way consistent with protecting society from a few who continue in the field of criminal activity.
This bill, in spite of the somewhat cynical approach of the hon. member for Timiskam-ing (Mr. Peters) will, in the light of experience so far due to the sharply increased use of pardons in the last year, do much to assist the people who are now being unjustly dealt with by society.

He said: Mr. Speaker, the amendments to the Excise Act contained in this bill are meant to facilitate, generally speaking, the administrative tasks of the department while ensuring that the provisions of the act are consistent with the ever changing technological conditions.
Several parts of the present act are carried over from the Internal Revenue Act and do not correspond anymore to the operations undertaken by licenced industries, where the use of storage and recovery systems based on data processing, automation and other electronic devices is an everyday reality.
Besides, the changes improve the wording of some clauses to make it agree with that of the Food and Drugs Act and Trade Marks Act.
The changes are in no way controversial and they will enable the department to show more administrative flexibility and reduce the cost of the supervision of industries regulated under this act, that is distilleries, breweries, tobacco and cigar manufacturers as well as other industries who use ethyl alcool in the manufacturing of their products such as perfume and vinegar.

You will notice that clause 30 of the bill will provide for the ex-warehousing of vodka

spirits by distillers, without age. The regulations which are made pursuant to the Food and Drugs Act and which provide identity standards for alcoholic beverages, permit the sale of vodka to consumers, without age; but under the Excise Act, section 149(3), domestic vodka is in the category of spirits which must be warehoused for at least two years before release from a distillery. Consequently, imported vodka is accorded an advantage over domestic vodka. It has been found that storage of vodka in metal tanks has no aging or maturing effect and that cost for inventory and storage facilities are unnecessarily paid for by the consumer. Mr. Speaker, the Auditor General, in its reports tabled in the House of Commons for the years 1967, 1968 and 1969, has stated that the department does not correctly apply the provisions of section 137(1). However, the department feels that it does.
This subsection of the act provides five alternative bases upon which duty on spirits shall he charged and computed and also provides for specific deductions or allowances for losses due to evaporation while the spirits were maturing in storage. The subsection has been amended to improve its wording and to facilitate its interpretation and more especially to remove the specific allowances and the 15-years maximum period of storage.
Competition on international markets requires that alcohol be stored for more than 15 years. The elimination of the 15-year limit will permit Canadian distillers to meet the competition of foreign distillers who sell spirits that have been stored for more than 15 years. Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak on Bill C-209, introduced by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cote).
I am happy to say at the outset-and pleased to point it out-that this is a good bill, although it is rather technical. It has some merits and anyone who has gone to the trouble of analyzing it and comparing it with the existing legislation feels that the minister is to be congratulated. I am doing it with all the more pleasure since I have always considered the Minister of National Revenue as a gifted man. He is more a statesman to me than a man given to small politics and I wish to pay him that tribute.
That being said, I come to the subject before us. I do not intend to use all the time I could be allowed but I should like to point out to the minister one particular point and I believe that the minister will agree with me on that.
Mr. Speaker, the object of this bill is to give more flexibility to the administration. Considering the existing Excise Act, one realizes-and I shall use here an old Quebec expression-"that a cow would not be able to find its calf there". That act is extremely complicated and outmoded and does not meet modern administrative needs, all the more so since we have to do here with a department that must resort to advanced technical methods.
The first purpose of the bill is to provide for a greater flexibility in the administration and this will certainly be achieved. As for the second purpose, it aims at reducing the costs of enforcing the law.
At the moment, there are almost as many inspectors in the department as there are taxpayers. The huge number of inspectors breeds complications and the administrative costs are extremely high.
By pruning a number of sections, and notably section 37, we shall help to reduce the cost of administering the law.

It is my duty to emphasize the importance of the general purposes of this bill which are to bring about administrative flexibility and to reduce administrative costs.
I find it very difficult, however, Mr. Speaker, to understand exactly what the minister has in mind when he talks about greater competition between Canadian and imported products.
Even if I did agree with the reasons for such a policy, it still appears as if the minister were encouraging a greater consumption of spirits in Canada.

Research conducted by Messrs. Moreau and Jorge of the Alcoholism and Drug Research Foundation shows that the sales of beer, wine and spirits in 1967 amounted to $1,346,442,000. Now, the statistics compiled by the staff of my department indicate that such sales in 1968 increased by $130,000,000.

Mr. Speaker, this is to some extent the particular point on which I wanted to draw the attention of the minister. It goes without saying that he is not directly responsible for that. He has to look after taxes which he collects in order to supply the government with the money required for its administration.
He has also to implement the Excise Act. Bill C-209 tends to put order in the administration, to reduce costs and to make the act more flexible in order to provide revenue for the government.

Because I know the minister well and because I am aware of his interest in the fight against alcoholism in Canada, I think that he is perhaps the cabinet nember who knows most about spirits consumption in Canada and that he is in a position, on account of his deep-felt humanitarianism, to compare the demand for and consumption of spirits in Canada with those in other countries. He also knows the big returns Canada gets from that industry. It is a pity, however, that alcoholism should cause such hardships in Canada. I take the opportunity of this debate to urge the minister to say, in his closing remarks, whether or not he is prepared to advise at least the cabinet to assign part of the $1,346 million which the government draws from the sales of spirits for the promotion, not of alcoholism, but of temperance.

Since the government derives revenues of over $1.5 billion from that source, I feel it to be the duty of every member of the House, whether he belongs to the opposition or to the government party, to urge the minister to devote a part of those funds to inform people on temperance and on the ill effects of consuming spirits.
By this amendment, the minister will have performed a good service to the government in collecting the taxes, putting the Department of National Revenue's house in order but unfortunately he will not only have collected money from taxpayers but also have taught them to use spirits.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 27 I asked the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) whether the government, in view of the announcement by Canadian Pacific Railway that 10 per cent of its clerical staff, amounting to between 500 and 800 workers could be laid off, was giving urgent consideration to bringing forward legislation based on the Freedman commission report. I was surprised that the Minister of Labour, who has spoken so often and so eloquently about his sympathy and support for the objectives of ordinary working people, answered as he did.
His answer was a complete rejection of my suggestion. It was the same kind of answer which we in this House heard from the former Minister of Labour who has been promoted to a high position in the province of British Columbia. He also used to tell us that these matters could be handled through negotiations between the unions concerned and their employers. The present Minister of Labour of course realizes the background of the Freedman commission hearings. He knows that the Freedman commission was appointed by a former Liberal government as a result of an illegal work stoppage caused by a unilaterial decision of Canadian National to reorganize the operation of its trains so that the operating staff of the railway would have to undertake longer rims.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
A stoppage would have meant phasing out the whole town of Machin in northern Ontario. Because of the inability to reach an agreement, an illegal work stoppage took place. The government appointed Mr. Justice Freedman to inquire into the cause of the
May 12, 1970	COMMONS
stoppage and to make recommendations. Mr. Justice Freedman brought forward a report in which he recommended that in cases of technological and other industrial conversion changes which have a substantial effect on the work force, an employer should be required to negotiate with the union: should there be no agreement, an employer would be barred from making the changes until the contract had expired and the union had regained the right to negotiate and, if necessary, strike. That is precisely what is taking place with the CPR at the present time. The CPR made a unilaterial decision to reduce its clerical work force by 10 per cent. I presume the reasons are the use of computers and other equipment which require a much smaller clerical staff.
The union has an agreement with the company under which a fund was set up to take care of lay-offs of workers as a result of technological change. Under that provision, when lay-offs occur the company is required to make supplementary payments to the workers affected. The company is taking the very narrow view that it is not necessary for them to give this kind of notice because it was not a technological change which led to the lay-offs. The minister was correct in his answer when he said that the union could take the matter to arbitration. The minister knows even better than I that arbitration takes time and that, more important, it will cost the union a substantial amount of money. I submit that all this could have been avoided had the government followed its expressed views and had introduced legislation implementing the 1965 report of Mr. Justice Freedman.
Some days later I asked a question and received a very curt reply and rejection from the minister. In an interview on the CTV program "Question Period" the minister indicated that the government will introduce this legislation this fall. I suggest to the minister that he should follow the slogan used by the employment service for many years, "Why wait for spring? Do it now." I suggest to the minister that there is still time before the House adjourns for the government to introduce this legislation which so often has been promised. The legislation could be passed before the summer recess.

The announcement by CPR to lay off clerical personnel across the country raised the question of whether this action is in violation of the job security, technological, operational and organizational change agreement between the company and the Brotherhood of Railway and Steamship Clerks.
The company contends that the decision to effect a 10 per cent reduction in clerical costs, which will result in lay-offs, is in accordance with the provisions of the agreement. The employees who qualify would be entitled to weekly lay-off benefits or severance payments, training or relocation expenses. The union contends that the company's decision is an organizational change which, in accordance with the provisions of the agreement, requires the company to give advance notice to the union of changes in working conditions, also the number of employees who would be adversely affected. Under the agreement there is provision for matters in dispute to be referred to arbitration. We understand that the union is preparing its case for submission in the arbitration procedure.
On the more general question raised, Mr. Speaker, concerning the introduction of legislation which would incorporate the recommendations of the Freedman report, the Minister of Labour on numerous occasions has indicated his intention to introduce provisions in legislation designed to deal with the kind of problems considered by Mr. Justice Freedman in his report. Had the hon. member been present this morning when the Department of Labour estimates were before the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration, he would have heard the minister reiterate that he hopes to introduce in the House this fall amendments to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act.
It is in this act we would logically look for action in respect of the issues raised by Freedman insofar as they relate to the collective bargaining process. Beyond this it does not seem appropriate to comment further at the present time.

maintopic: CONSUMER AFFAIRS-SURVEY OF COST AND QUALITY OF CAR REPAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few days ago on the Orders of the Day I asked the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) whether his depart-
6894	COMMONS DEBATES	May 12, 1979
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion ment was conducting a survey of the automobile repair industry in Canada. His reply was "No." Believing, as I do, that this is a matter of great importance to millions of Canadian consumers, I have taken the opportunity of raising the question again tonight. I was somewhat surprised that the minister should say his department was not looking into this subject. It is more than a year ago that I asked whether his department would consider initiating in this country an investigation similar to the one being carried on in the United States before a Senate committee. The minister replied that he was aware of the United States inquiry and that he was obtaining a copy of the evidence placed before it so that he might judge its appropriateness to Canadian conditions. In view of the fact that some rather horrendous facts and figures about car repairs were brought to light in the course of that investigation, I am surprised that the minister has not taken any action in this area.
Again, on February 2 of this year I pursued the matter of complaints made by a consumer organization, the Automobile Protective Association of Canada, concerning alleged shortcomings of car repair clinics in Canada. At that time the minister said that he was not prepared to give me an answer; his department had been studying the matter very carefully but the jurisdiction of the federal government was somewhat doubtful except when fraud under the Criminal Code was involved, and he did not think the complaints referred to actually involved fraud.
Mr. Speaker, on February 5, just three days after the minister's reply, the Ontario Law Reports revealed that an Ottawa judge had ordered an Esso car clinic to pay $250 in damages to a motorist who accepted its diagnosis and bought a used car which soon broke down. The learned judge found that the consumer had been "led to believe that the engine of the car was in sound condition, calling for only very minor repairs." He was satisfied that no thorough examination of the engine had in fact been made. Since that time we have heard nothing further as to possible action by the Consumer Affairs Department to protect people who need their cars repaired.
In raising the matter now I wish to put a few figures on record to show the importance to Canadian consumers of car repair costs and

quality. I urge the minister to confer with his colleague the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) on the aspect of motor vehicle safety. This is a matter which affects both the lives and the pocketbooks of hundreds of thousands of Canadians. It costs Canadians approximately $27 a month just to repair and to maintain their cars. This amounts to about $2 billion a year. The car repair industry embraces about six million cars in Canada.
e (9:40 p.m.)
In the United States, the Senate inquiry was told that car repairs cost approximately $25 billion a year, and it was said that this was comparable with what Americans spend yearly for new cars. The auto repair business, according to an article in Canadian magazine of March 8, 1969, is "a jungle". This article quotes the head of Quebec's Automotive Service Association as saying: "When you take your car in to be fixed in this province, you really take your chances". There are a great many factors involved in the car repair problem, and this affects the car insurance business and the rates that people have to pay for car insurance.
In view of the magnitude of the car repair business, the vast number of Canadians affected, the high cost of and many complaints about the quality of repairs, and finally the safety factor involved, I have taken the privilege tonight of once more raising this question. I urge the minister to initiate in this country a similar investigation to that which was carried out in the United States.
